{{Short description|Type of plane wave}}
[[File:Plane wave wavefronts 3D.svg|thumb|right|300px|The [[wavefront]]s of a traveling plane wave in three-dimensional space.]]

In [[mathematics]] and [[physics]], a '''traveling plane wave'''<ref>{{Citation |last=Tohyama |first=Mikio |chapter=Waves and Speed of Sound in the Air |date=2011 |title=Sound and Signals |pages=89–102 |editor-last=Tohyama |editor-first=Mikio |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-20122-6_6 |access-date=2024-08-05 |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-20122-6_6#citeas |isbn=978-3-642-20122-6|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> is a special case of [[plane wave]], namely a [[field (physics)|field]] whose evolution in time can be described as simple translation of its values at a constant ''[[Phase velocity|wave speed]]'' <math>c</math>, along a fixed ''[[direction of propagation]]'' <math>\vec n</math>.

Such a field can be written as  
:<math>F(\vec x, t)=G\left(\vec x \cdot \vec n - c t\right)\,</math>
where <math>G(u)</math> is a function of a single real parameter <math>u = d - c t</math>.  The function <math>G</math> describes the '''profile''' of the wave, namely the value of the field at time <math>t = 0</math>, for each displacement <math>d = \vec x \cdot \vec n</math>.  For each displacement <math>d</math>, the moving plane perpendicular to <math>\vec n</math> at distance <math>d + c t</math> from the origin is called a '''[[wavefront]]'''.  This plane too travels along the direction of propagation <math>\vec n</math> with velocity <math>c</math>; and the value of the field is then the same, and constant in time, at every one of its points.

The wave <math>F</math> may be a [[scalar field|scalar]] or [[vector field]]; its values are the values of <math>G</math>.

A [[sinusoidal plane wave]] is a special case, when <math>G(u)</math> is a [[sinusoidal]] function of <math>u</math>.

==Properties==
A traveling plane wave can be studied by ignoring the dimensions of space perpendicular to the vector  <math>\vec n</math>; that is, by considering the wave <math>F(z\vec n,t) = G(z - ct)</math> on a one-dimensional medium, with a single position coordinate <math>z</math>.

For a scalar traveling plane wave in two or three dimensions, the gradient of the field is always collinear with the direction <math>\vec n</math>; specifically, <math>\nabla F(\vec x,t) = \vec n G'(\vec x \cdot \vec n - ct)</math>, where <math>G'</math> is the derivative of <math>G</math>.   Moreover, a traveling plane wave <math>F</math> of any shape satisfies the [[partial differential equation]]<!-- More: divergent, curl, laplacian...-->
:<math>\nabla F = -\frac{\vec n}{c}\frac{\partial F}{\partial t}</math>

Plane traveling waves are also special solutions of the [[wave equation]] in an homogeneous medium.
